title: RCMP officers acted appropriately in shooting of Onoway man, judge rules
subtitle: Officers not trained with Tasers at time of shooting, inquiry hears
article: Two RCMP officers who killed an Onoway man who approached them with a knife made "reasonable" decisions in order to protect themselves and others, a judge has ruled.
A public fatality inquiry report released on Monday paints a picture of the last moments of Darby Mahon's life, just before the 49-year-old was shot by the RCMP on Jan.11, 2012.

Mahon, who was described by witnesses as "intoxicated and angry," confronted his daughter's boyfriend after the couple had an argument earlier that evening. Both men lived in the same apartment building.

Mahon kicked in the door to the boyfriend's apartment and went after the man, who locked himself in the apartment's bedroom with his mother. Mahon struck the bedroom door with a machete. When his daughter took the weapon away, he returned to his own apartment and got another knife.

When the two RCMP officers arrived at the apartment, they found Mahon struggling with a woman. She retreated into another room and officers ordered Mahon to put the knife down. According to the report, Mahon instead approached one officer, saying "one way or another I'm gonna kill him."

The officers were not able to back away. They both fired their guns when Mahon was about five feet away, and he was shot twice in the abdomen. An ambulance was called and one officer applied pressure to the wound until EMS arrived.

During the fatality inquiry, an RCMP expert testified that the officers acted appropriately when they shot Mahon. Neither officer was equipped with a Taser, Judge Jacqueline Schaffter heard. And since the apartment was an enclosed space with many people inside, the officers decided against using pepper spray.

Schaffter ruled that the officers shot Mahon to protect themselves and other people in the apartment. One of Mahon's daughters called for more training to allow RCMP officers to better respond to incidents involving the mentally ill, as well as more training with Tasers and better record-keeping.
Schaffter agreed that the changes would be beneficial, but said none would prevent similar deaths in the future. In the end, she made no recommendations in the report.
